newsitem.title: USA: Maine Yankee safe but has problems - review team.
newsitem.headline: Maine Yankee safe but has problems - review team.

text.p: The Maine Yankee nuclear power plant is safe enough to operate, but has major weaknesses, a special review team said Friday.
"Overall, we felt performance was adequate for safe operation of Maine Yankee," said Ellis Merschoff, who headed an independent safety assessment team.
But he outlined several problems which would have made the plant dangerous if it had a cooling water accident.
In one case, a wire that had been mistakenly removed "would have raised the risk for that plant by about six percent," Merschoff told the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.

The special review overseen by the NRC was requested by Maine Gov. Angus King after the commissions's inspector general charged that regulators had failed to check safety tests properly on a key cooling system.
While the overall "quality of maintenance at the plant was good," Merschoff said "the trend is in the wrong direction."

Maintenance weaknesses posed "significant problems," he said, pointing to declining condition of feed water pumps, leaking valves, and an auxhiliary pump, which Commissioner Nils Diaz called "a very, very significant safety component."
"The scope of their testing program was inadequate," Merschoff said in a briefing to the NRC. "The corrective action is a key problem."
"The plant was willing to live with a large number of workarounds," said Edward Jordan, manager of the assessment, describing moves to work around problems rather than fix them.
The assessment team blamed management for shelving some maintenance activities to cut costs.
"Economic pressure to be a low cost energy producer has limited available resources to address corrective actions and plant improvements," Merschoff said.
"Management appears complacent with the current level of safety performance, and there does not appear to be a clear incentive for improvement," the review said.

The plant, which the NRC had limited to 90 percent of capacity during the inspection, could be operated at its current 2440 megawatts thermal power, but should not be increased to 2700, Merschoff said.
Maine Yankee's president, Charles Frizzle, has said he would ensure the plant ran safely.
"We will devote whatever resources necessary to operate the plant safely, or we will not operate it at all," he said recently, according to Maine Yankee spokeswoman Maureen Brown.
"We've developed an excellent action plan in response to the ISA (independent safety assessment)," Brown said.
The company must submit a formal response to the report by December 10.
Maine Yankee is 38 percent owned by Central Maine Power Co, 20 percent each by New England Electric System and Northeast Utilities, and 22 percent by other New England utilities.
